state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of the number line as a road trip. You start at -12, drive 10 units to the right, then drive b units to the left to end up at -7. When you're driving backwards, you don't count the starting point again, just like when you're driving from a negative number to a positive one. So, what do you think \( b \) should be to get to -7?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get what you're saying about the road trip. So, if I start at -12 and go 10 units to the right, I end up at -2, right? But then if I go back to -7, I'm not sure how far that is. Is it just 5 units back?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it like this: when you're driving back on the road trip, you don't count the starting point again. So, if you're at -2 and you need to get back to -7, how many units do you need to go in the opposite direction to reach your destination?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I'm at -2 and I need to get to -7, I guess I have to go back 5 units, right? But I'm still confused about how that relates to \( b \). Is \( b \) just the distance I need to go back, or is it something else?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses a road trip analogy but never directly addresses the student's misconception about arrows starting at zero, and by Turn 4 the student still doesn't understand what b represents despite correctly calculating the distance.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete real-world analogy (road trip with driving forward and backward) throughout the dialogue to help the student understand the abstract concept of movement on a number line, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
